newsitem.title: CHINA: Chubb says foreign insurers no harm to China.
newsitem.headline: Chubb says foreign insurers no harm to China.

text.p: U.S.-based insurer Chubb Corp said on Wednesday that foreign underwriters posed no major threat to Chinese insurance firms, and predicted that Beijing would gradually open the sector to overseas companies.

A Chubb-backed survey showed China would likely follow patterns set by other Asian nations such as Japan, where the insurance market had been open for 30 years but foreign insurers had only a three percent share, said Ian Lancaster, Chubb's manager for the China region.

The 1996 survey of 437 companies in Beijing had found that 63 percent of those with property insurance said they would not, or would probably not, switch insurance firms within the next two years, Lancaster told Reuters in an interview.
Some 69 percent of companies with liability insurance said they definitely or probably would not switch from their current supplier, he said.
Lancaster said he hoped the survey results would help ease Beijing's fears about subjecting fledgling domestic firms to competition from more experienced foreign companies.
"There has been a lot of emotion in China about whether the insurance market should be opened up to foreigners," he said.
"The government need not worry as much about foreign entry as it thinks it should," he said. "It's going to be a lot tougher for foreign insurers to break into the China market."
"The China market is a huge market," he said, adding that premium income in 1996 was about $8.0 billion, of which foreign insurers had but a few percent.
The survey showed 87 percent of insurance clients said they wanted more choice, Lancaster said.
"The Chinese consumer is starting to recognise that the way to buy is to shop around, and the more choice you've got, the better off they are," he said.
There was no doubt China would eventually grant licences to more overseas insurers, Lancaster said, but added that it would be a gradual process.
Scores of foreign insurance firms have opened representative offices in China but only a handful are allowed to issue policies.
Those firms include Winterthur Swiss Insurance Co, American International Assurance Co Ltd, a part of the American International Group, and Tokio Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd.
Chubb now had representative offices in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen, but Lancaster said he did not know when the corporate insurer would win a full business licence.
"We would suggest to the government that it's time to probably experiment by licensing a specialist company, i.e., a company like Chubb," he said.

Opening its insurance sector to foreign firms is one of a string of demands on China as it negotiates entry to the World Trade Organisation, and the issue is expected to come up when bilateral negotiations resume in May, diplomats have said.

China has yet to come up with even a proposal on opening its jealously guarded insurance market -- one of the top demands of several nations involved in the bilateral talks, including the United States, Europe and Japan.
